newsitem.title: UK: S&N, Burton set to be ousted from FTSE.
newsitem.headline: S&N, Burton set to be ousted from FTSE.

text.p: Two more banking giants are set to muscle into Britain's FTSE 100 share index in its quarterly shake-up to be decided at the close of business on Tuesday.

Recently-floated Halifax Plc and Alliance & Leicester were poised to elbow out drugs group Smith & Nephew and retailer Burtons, beefing up the bank sector's already weighty presence in the blue-chip index.

Halifax and A&L, both former building societies which converted to banks and joined London's stock exchange over the last two months, will easily qualify for inclusion in the elite ranks of Britain's biggest publicly quoted companies.

Halifax has a market capitalisation of around 18.8 billion pounds ($30.7 billion), making it the third biggest of Britain's quoted banks, while Alliance & Leicester comes in at around 12.4 billion pounds.
They will officially join the index on June 23.

Smith & Nephew and Burton, which languish at the bottom of the index with a market capitalisation of around 1.9 billion pounds each, have no chance of standing in their way as the banks charge into the FTSE 100.
The only hope the two companies have of staying in the index is by overtaking the next smallest companies -- Imperial Tobacco and Tate & Lyle, capitalised at around 2.0 billion pounds.
But barring any dramatic price movements later in the session, this is unlikely.

A company qualifies for automatic inclusion in the FTSE 100 if it ranks among the top 90 in terms of market capitalisation at the close of business on one of the four annual dates on which the index constituents are revised. It then replaces the lowest ranking index constituent.
Alternatively, if a stock in the index falls below 110 in the list it will be replaced by the next largest company. This quarter's decision will be made on the basis of Tuesday's closing prices.

Williams Holdings Plc, Compass Group Plc and MEPC Plc are all snapping at the heels of the FTSE laggards, but analysts say that unless prices change significantly before the close, they will fail to gain access to the blue-chip party.

There is more than just honour at stake in being included -- institutions running funds that track the FTSE 100 must build up holdings of companies which are on course to get into the index, and sell those that drop out.
The two new boys will further raise the presence of financials in the index, even before the imminent flotation of insurer Norwich Union NRU.CN and the Woolwich building society WOO.CN..
Retail banks already have a weighting of 18.34 percent in the FTSE 100 index, according to Reuters Securities 3000 data, while financials as a whole have a weighting of 24.09 percent.
This is smaller than the weighting of financial stocks in Germany's DAX index -- 28.58 percent -- but greater than their 18.34 percent weighting in France's CAC 40.
The banking sector has played a crucial role in driving the FTSE's record-breaking rally of recent months -- in the past year it has outperformed the FTSE 100 as a whole by 35 percent.
Without the strong performance of banks, and their significant weighting in the FTSE, the performance of the index would not have been nearly as impressive, analysts say. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
